newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless claims fell in latest week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless claims fell in latest week.

text.p: U.S. Labor Department report of initial state jobless benefit claims, seasonally adjusted.
Week Ended Initial Claims 4-Week Avg. Continued Claims
R-Revised, Feb 15 Initial Claims from 305,000, Feb 22 4-Week Average from 313,250, Feb 15 from 317,250, Feb 15 Continued Claims from 2,412,000.
Wall Street economists had forecast initial jobless claims of 317,000 in the March 1 week.
The four-week moving average in the March 1 week was at its lowest level since May 13, 1989, when it was 309,750.
Labor said seven states reported decreases in claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended Feb 22, the latest period for which data are available.
They were New York, with 2,889 fewer new filings; Ohio, with 2,597; Pennsylvania, with 2,209; Arkansas, with 1,513; South Carolina, with 1,351; Maryland, with 1,153; and Michigan, with 1,133.
New York and Arkansas linked the drop to a shorter work week due to the President's Day holiday.
Pennsylvania reported fewer layoffs in the construction, trade, and lumber and wood industries, while South Carolina said it had fewer layoffs in the apparel industry.

Maryland reported fewer layoffs in the publishing, optical goods, trade, and service industries. Michigan had fewer layoffs in various industries throughout the state. Ohio gave no reason for its decline.
Six states reported increases in claims exceeding 1,000 in the Feb 22 week.
They were Massachusetts, with 3,545 additional new filings; North Carolina, with 2,345; California, with 1,645; Connecticut, 1,422, Rhode Island, with 1,152; and Texas, with 1,085.
Massachusetts had layoffs in the service industry, while North Carolina reported layoffs in the construction and textile industries.

Rhode Island attributed the increase in claims to layoffs in the trade and service industries and in manufacturing, while Texas said it had layoffs in the rubber and electrical equipment industries. California and Connecticut gave no explanation for their increases.
